conceptTag: Judging a hire after one great interview
readerTitle: The candidate everyone loved after one interview
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장재 공장 교대조 관리자, 소프트웨어 스타트업 시니어 엔지니어) + 채용 연구 일반론
insight: 인상적인 면접 한 번은 한 가지 능력의 증거일 뿐이다. 직무 요건을 하나씩 나누고, 윗사람 의견을 듣기 전에 각자 점수를 매겨야 판단이 섞이지 않는다.
misconception: 면접에서 확실히 좋았으면 좋은 사람이다. 대표나 가장 경험 많은 사람이 좋다고 하면 그게 맞다.

sources.text: Thorndike, E. L. (1920). A constant error in psychological ratings. Journal of Applied Psychology.
Schmidt, F. L., & Hunter, J. E. (1998). The validity and utility of selection methods in personnel psychology. Psychological Bulletin.
공장과 스타트업 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 5번 카드의 '구조화 면접이 비구조화 면접보다 직무 성과를 더 잘 예측한다'는 Schmidt & Hunter(1998) 등 메타분석의 일반적 결론입니다. 구체적 수치(타당도 계수)는 일부러 쓰지 않았습니다. 이후 Sackett 외(2022) 재분석에서도 구조화 면접이 상위권인지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
후광 효과의 기원을 Thorndike(1920)로 표기했습니다. 카드 본문에는 연구 내용을 직접 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The candidate everyone loved after one interview
body: You run a packaging plant. You need a night-shift supervisor for 40 people. Dana walks in, tells sharp stories about fixing a messy line at a bigger company, and makes the panel laugh twice.
Forty-five minutes later, the room is ready to hire. That feeling is exactly when to slow down.

image.label: Interview panel smiling at a confident candidate
image.brief: 공장 사무실의 면접 장면. 지원자 한 명이 손짓하며 이야기하고 면접관 세 명이 웃고 있음. 지원자 주변에 은은한 빛(후광) 효과. 창밖으로 포장 라인이 보임. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: What do you do next?
body: Dana is the best interview you've had in months. Two other candidates are still in the process. Dana mentions another offer.

options.text: Make an offer today before you lose Dana
options.feedback: You gain speed but bet on one strength. This is the **halo effect**: great storytelling makes you assume great scheduling, safety and coaching too.

options.text: Call two references and ask how Dana handled problems
options.feedback: Better evidence, but references are chosen by the candidate and often glow. The halo can follow Dana into those calls.

options.text: List what the job needs, and check each item for all three candidates the same way
options.feedback: This breaks the halo into parts. You may still pick Dana, but now for reasons you can name.

cards.title: One strength, three blanks.
body: The interview proved Dana communicates well. Everything else was assumed from that.

cards.title: The owner speaks up first.
body: In the debrief, the plant owner says, "Best candidate I've seen in years." Two managers nod. The safety lead looks unsure but says nothing.

options.text: Let the owner set the direction. It's their plant
options.feedback: Fast and comfortable, but this is **authority bias**. Others shape their views to match the boss, and the safety lead's doubt is lost.

options.text: Everyone writes scores first, then shares. The most senior person speaks last
options.feedback: You get each person's real view before rank pulls it in one direction. It costs ten minutes and a little awkwardness.

options.text: Open discussion, then a show of hands
options.feedback: It feels fair, but people still hear the owner first. The vote can just count how many followed authority.

cards.title: Split the person into parts.
body: Both biases blend many judgments into one. The cure is to pull them apart.

Write down three to five things the job needs. Ask every candidate the same question for each, ideally a real task, like planning a shift from last week's orders. Score each item separately, with a note on the evidence.
Decades of hiring research point the same way: **structured interviews** predict job performance better than free-flowing conversations.

image.label: Scorecard with separate rows for each job need
image.brief: 평가표 인포그래픽. 행: "Shift planning", "Safety", "Coaching crews", "Communication". 열: 지원자 A, B, C. 각 칸에 점수와 짧은 근거 메모. 한 지원자가 Communication만 높고 나머지는 비어 있는 모습을 강조.

cards.title: Don't swing to distrusting charm.
body: Sometimes the great interview is real evidence. For a supervisor, clear communication is part of the job. Count it, just don't let it fill in the other rows.
Structure also costs time, and strong candidates do take other offers. Keep it fast: one work task, one scorecard, a decision within days. Structure lowers your error rate. It doesn't remove it.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: You're hiring a senior engineer. The candidate spent five years at a famous tech company. Your co-founder and CTO says after one call, "She's a lock. Let's skip the rest."

options.text: Hire her. The pedigree and the CTO's judgment are enough
options.feedback: Two biases stack here: the famous brand creates a **halo**, and the CTO's rank adds **authority bias**. Neither tests how she works in your codebase.

options.text: Run a short paid pairing session on your real code. Two engineers score it before hearing the CTO's view
options.feedback: You test the actual job and protect independent views. It adds a few days, which is cheap next to a bad senior hire.

options.text: Ask the CTO to do a second, longer call
options.feedback: More time helps, but one enthusiastic interviewer tends to look for proof they were right.

cards.title: One great interview proves one thing.
body: Used here: the **halo effect** (one strength colors everything) and **authority bias** (the senior voice sets the answer).
**Try it today:** for your next open role, write the three things the job needs most. Before any debrief, have each interviewer score them alone.
